articles.title: The most underrated player in the NBA? Ty Jerome makes a strong case in Memphis
articles.summary: Jerome is starring on a surprise Grizzlies team and pressure-testing the predictive value of all-in-one metrics.
articles.body:
Go ahead and build out your top 10 players in the league. You could start with scoring champs like Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Stephen Curry and Kevin Durant. Perhaps dominant bigs suit your fancy like Nikola Jokić, Victor Wembanyama and Joel Embiid. Maybe go with chess grandmasters like LeBron James, Luka Dončić and Giannis Antetokounmpo. That's even before we get to ruthless bucket-getters like Jalen Brunson, Tyrese Maxey and Jayson Tatum.

That's 12. You can bet a host of other All-Stars would like a word, too.

But a name that you probably didn't submit is one that many advanced metrics loudly claim absolutely belongs in that top-10 conversation:

Ahead of the season — before the NBA announced Jerome as the Western Conference Player of the Week — Estimated Plus-Minus pegged the 29-year-old as the ninth-best offensive player in the league . DARKO was bullish too, ranking him 14th, ahead of future Hall of Famers like Durant and Antetokounmpo. This, despite Jerome not even ranking in the Top 100 lists for ESPN , The Ringer and CBS Sports . Surely, the calculators were glitching, right?

And then the season started. In Memphis' dominant opening night win over the Utah Jazz, Jerome scored 45 points , the most the franchise had ever seen in a season opener — a performance so captivating that he generated MVP chants from the FedEx Forum faithful.

Meet the most underrated player in the NBA, who is leading the 4-0 Grizzlies and simultaneously pressure-testing the predictive value of all-in-one metrics.

Jerome doesn't look like your typical 30-point scorer. He can't dunk. At least he has never dunked in an NBA game. Or, it seems, in college. There was once a Reddit forum from his time with the Virginia Cavaliers that asked, "Have you ever seen Ty Jerome dunk?" It turned up … nothing.

His ground-bound 6-foot-5 frame hardly looks carved out of marble. He's not winning any foot races either.

And yet: no one can seem to stop him. Through four games, all wins, Jerome is averaging 29.8 points, 6.3 assists and just 1.8 turnovers. He is fully in his bag, slaloming through defenses with unpredictable deceleration and his signature impeccable touch.

There are scorers who sprinkle in floaters, and then there is Jerome. According to Sportradar tracking, Jerome has an NBA-high 29 floaters or "runners" this season, 10 more than the next-highest guy. When Jerome comes off a screen, he waits for the big man defender to retreat to the rim and wall off a lob to Jerome's big. That's when he poofs the ball into the air, and usually sees it fall into the cup. These are layups for him. He has made 59% of these floaters, which, actually, is a couple percentage ticks higher than your average NBA layup.

Jerome is driving defenses mad with his stop-and-go speed toggling. He is averaging 8.3 free throws per game, more than twice as many as he did last season. If you get your hand caught in the cookie jar, he'll draw a foul. Off balance and lean too much on him? Whistle.

In Monday's win over the Jazz, he got to the line "only" seven times and scored 15 points, a third of what Jerome dropped on opening night against the same team. After losing to Memphis a second time, Utah coach Will Hardy praised his team's defense on Jerome. Meanwhile, the Grizzlies scored 121 points per 100 possessions with Jerome on the floor — a rate on par with the best offense in the league. On a Jerome off night, the offense is still elite.

Taylor Snarr did. Guys like Jerome keep the former Utah Jazz analytics guru up at night.

The proprietor behind the DunksAndThrees.com analytics hub, Snarr designed his flagship metric Estimated Plus-Minus following his four-year stint with the Jazz as a way to help accurately predict NBA games ( it has shown to be the sharpest among the top advanced metrics) . Simply put, it blends a player's box score numbers with on-court/off-court data with fancy adjustments to account for teammate quality, injuries, substitutions and opponent quality while peppering in player-tracking data. It has been a go-to metric for analytically inclined writers and data-driven front offices who need a handy guide for player value.

Jerome has long been an outlier for EPM, the Salt Lake City-based data scientist says. The list of top weapons is a crowd of future Hall of Famers, and then there's Jerome, who has bounced around the league more than the basketball itself.

The former No. 24 pick in the 2019 draft was rerouted twice during the draft process, first from Philly to Boston and then eventually to Phoenix, where he lasted for only his rookie season. Traded in the Chris Paul deal of 2021, the Oklahoma City Thunder gave him a shot where he shuttled back and forth from OKC's G League team. In 2022, he was traded to the Houston Rockets and waived almost immediately. The Golden State Warriors picked him up and he played about half the season.

Jerome found what he thought was a trusty home in Cleveland. At the start of the 2024-25 season, his offensive output was rated in the 42nd percentile, or just below average. But then he took off. Unsustainably so. In fact, at the time, Snarr used Jerome as an example of the difference between EPM's two metrics, one that was backward looking ( how good has this player been? ) vs. one that had an eye to the future ( how good is this player going forward? ).

"Ty Jerome has shot 55% from 3, 66% from midrange this season--impressive! Will it continue? Not at those rates. He ranks 8 in Season EPM so far and 77 in EPM (up from 309!). EPM is optimized to measure real improvement."

In other words, Snarr's model wasn't totally convinced that Jerome's ultra hot start in 2024-25 was sustainable. But then he kept it up and then some. Jerome averaged a career-high 12.5 points off the bench for the top-seeded Cavs and finished third in the Sixth Man of the Year race.

Snarr was stunned at the results. Jerome began the season as a fringe player in the NBA. By the end of it, Snarr's model saw Jerome become an offensive weapon that ranked in the 95th percentile, among names like Anthony Edwards, LeBron James and James Harden. That was forward-looking, not just in the rear-view mirror.

Ty Jerome, a superstar offensive player? When I asked Snarr if he was worried about being wrong about Jerome he said, "Yes, absolutely," and admits he has lost sleep over the surging Memphis point guard. From time to time, outliers like Jerome have given Snarr the stare-at-the-ceiling treatment, causing him to question whether the algorithm needed to be tweaked. Snarr wondered if the model was missing something, as if Jerome's unique game was an illusory siren that EPM couldn't resist.

Snarr decided not to tinker with the model. That summer, the Grizzlies signed Jerome to a three-year, $27 million deal. A good deal for Jerome, who had struggled to catch on, but the salary was on par with someone who is a rotation player, not a singular offensive engine like Snarr's model had envisioned. Snarr was hopeful Jerome could break out again even on a team that still had Ja Morant.

At the start of the 2025-26 season, Jerome suffered a severe calf injury that sidelined him until late January. But once he got back on the floor, Jerome was spectacular — as predicted. Grizzlies coach Tuomas Iisalo gushed about Jerome's game.

Jerome "doesn't look like the most explosive guy, but he gets to his spots on the floor because he reads so well the body language of not only his own defender but also the helping defenders," Iisalo said in February. "He's actually so good that he can manipulate [defenders] to get out of the space that he wants to create or get into the space that he wants to create for someone else."

On a languishing team, Jerome registered a whopping 31.3 points and 9 assists per 36 minutes. That was relief for Snarr; the EPM model seemed to be calibrated properly as Jerome was truly elite. A little too elite, perhaps, in the eyes of Memphis, which had already fallen 10 games below .500 by the time Jerome returned. Whether it was ping-pong optimization or injury management, Jerome went on to start 15 games last season, but never played more than 25 minutes and almost never played in consecutive games. With visions of the No. 1 pick in sight, the Grizzlies shut down Jerome with 11 games to go.

When Morant got traded this offseason, another Jerome test would finally come. The big one. He'd finally get to start and show what he can do running an NBA team, a role EPM had envisioned.

In the opening week of this season, Jerome has been every bit the offensive engine that Snarr's model had predicted over a year ago. According to Snarr, Jerome is a darling of EPM because he blends self-created, frequent and efficient scoring with the ability to make plays for teammates with low turnovers. "This," Snarr says, "is the typical statistical profile of offensive stars in EPM."

In Snarr's view, Jerome's analytical story reminds him of LaMelo Ball, who was rated as a superstar offensive player over the years by EPM although the wins didn't quite take off until halfway through last season. Snarr also believes Jerome echoes the early days of Nikola Jokić in Denver (though Snarr isn't predicting multiple MVPs for Jerome, who is almost 30 years old).

The advanced metrics saw Jokić in his rookie season as a future star, with EPM predecessors like box plus-minus and real plus-minus ranking Jokić among the most impactful players in the league. Yet Jokić fought for minutes with JJ Hickson and Jusuf Nurkić. We know how that story ended. The numbers were clairvoyant in their belief in Jokić's game.

Jerome has enjoyed a soft schedule with opponents like Utah (twice), Golden State and Sacramento. On Thursday, the Grizzlies will face a tougher test against a Portland team that is 3-0. But after years of futility and controversy in Memphis, Jerome has made Grizzlies fans believers again.

Leading one of only three 4-0 teams in the NBA, Jerome has ascended higher than even EPM's rosy preseason projections. Jerome has now become the fifth -highest-rated offensive weapon in the game, vaulting past Kawhi Leonard, Tyrese Haliburton and, yes, LaMelo Ball. Overall, Snarr's predictive EPM places Jerome as the ninth-best player in the league with his defense taken into account — a guy major media outlets didn't have in their Top 100 weeks ago. With Western Conference Player of the Week honors to start the season, the accolades are finally coming in. If the numbers are to be trusted, the Ty Jerome experience is just getting started.

images.caption: The Western Conference Player of the Week, Ty Jerome is averaging 29.8 points, 6.3 assists and just 1.8 turnovers for the 4-0 Grizzlies. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) (Ezra Shaw via Getty Images)

articles.title: Women’s Sports Bar Owners: Matinee WNBA Finals Game a ‘Slap in the Face’
articles.summary: The Game 6 reschedule will likely mean thousands in lost revenue.
articles.body:
Moments after the WNBA rescheduled Game 6 of the Finals to a matinee, Clarissa Flores shared her surprise on Instagram. "A WNBA Finals game at 12:30 p.m. on a Thursday. Are you serious?" said Flores , the owner of Level Sporting Club, a Chicago-based women's sports bar that opened earlier this year.

On Monday afternoon, the WNBA announced it was pushing the game forward from 8 p.m. to 12:30 p.m. ET Thursday, allowing the Atlanta Dream to host the game at the 17,000-seat State Farm Arena rather than the 3,500-seat Gateway Center. The Hawks, who operate State Farm Arena, have a regular-season game Thursday night.

Many people were surprised by the WNBA's decision to move a Finals game—especially a potential title-clincher—so early. The Golden State Valkyries, who are up 3–2 in the series, would win their first title in franchise history with a win Thursday—and the game tips off at 9:30 a.m. in San Francisco.

In her social media post, Flores expressed how the early game affects all WNBA fans, as many will be at work or school during the game. For her business, she said WNBA Finals games "help keep the lights on."

"We spend all year telling people to show up for women's basketball, then on one of the biggest stages in the world, we make it even harder for them to show up. We're putting our money, our livelihoods, our future behind women's sports. … We need the people making the decisions to match that same commitment that we're giving," she said.

Front Office Sports spoke with multiple women's sports bar owners , who say that while they understand the league's logistical difficulties, the WNBA's decision negatively affects their businesses and sends a poor message to fans.

"To have this be what might be the last game of the Finals feels like such a slap in the face, and shows that they really don't care about us being able to watch the game," Chandler Robertson, owner of Blazers in Brooklyn, New York, told FOS .

Jenny Nguyen, founder of The Sports Bra in Portland, Oregon, said in a statement to FOS that there could be negative consequences for potentially sacrificing TV viewership of what is currently on pace to be the league's most-watched Finals ever: "When you schedule a Finals game at a time that keeps people from watching, it absolutely will hurt the numbers. Then those numbers risk being used as evidence that the audience isn't there. That's a frustrating cycle, and it's one that everyone in women's AND men's sports should be working together to break."

Jen Barnes, owner of Rough & Tumble in Seattle, told FOS she's not sure whether she'll be able to open for a 9:30 a.m. tip on the West Coast. "We normally open at 4 p.m. on weekdays. We're pulling in different schedules as it is for these games, but my kitchen team is not able to be on-site for a 9:30 a.m. tip-off," Barnes said.

She usually makes $10,000 to $15,000 between Rough & Tumble's two locations for a weeknight WNBA Finals game, revenue she may lose due to the Game 6 morning tip-off time. She said her business has seen "lines down the street" to get in for WNBA Finals games, particularly because of the many Valkyries fans in Seattle, but she doesn't expect the same crowd this time around.

"I think it's a huge underservice to the WNBA fan at the minimum, and it's an unfortunate revenue loss for all the places that play these games," Barnes said.

Women's sports bars in San Francisco (Rikki's) and Atlanta (Jolene Jolene) did not respond to an inquiry for this story.

Blazers in Brooklyn will be open for the early afternoon game on the East Coast, but Robertson said she expects turnout to be less than half of a primetime game. The WNBA Finals are core to her business; she said that for Game 5, Blazers made "more than triple" the revenue it would normally generate on a Monday.

Flores's Level Sporting Club announced late Monday that it will open for Thursday's 11:30 a.m. CT tip, branding it as a remote-work function on its social media. Speaking to FOS , Flores said it's the first time her bar has ever opened on a weekday morning.

"Having to open at 11, lunchtime for a Game 6 is one of the most absurd things I've ever heard," Flores said. "But we are going to do it because we're going to stand up for women's sports."

articles.title: NBA Insider Drops 'Cryptic' Thunder Intel on Potential Targets After Williams, Wallace Injuries
articles.summary: As the Oklahoma City Thunder deal with injuries to both Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace that are expected to keep them out indefinitely, it wouldn't be shocking if the team made a big move to bolster the roster around Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Chet Holmgren.
articles.body:
As the Oklahoma City Thunder deal with injuries to both Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace that are expected to keep them out indefinitely, it wouldn't be shocking if the team made a big move to bolster the roster around Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Chet Holmgren.

"And the one thing too is—and you guys noticed, like the McCain trade last year—like they identify a certain player that fits in that locker room, and also that fits within that style on the court," ESPN's Bobby Marks said during the most recent episode of The Hoop Collective podcast (17:53 mark). "Because they're not big on adding from the outside there."

ESPN's Brian Windhorst quickly followed that up.

"And this is one thing that I've talked to executives about, and I don't mean to be cryptic, but I'm being cryptic," he noted. "If you're going to, if they're going to acquire a player, would not be a surprise if they acquire a player they've already had."

Windy's comments will obviously invite speculation.

Some former Thunder players who could feasibly return at some point include Aaron Wiggins or Lu Dort on the Atlanta Hawks; Isaiah Joe on the Detroit Pistons; Jerami Grant on the Memphis Grizzlies; Dennis Schröder on the Charlotte Hornets; and Ousmane Dieng on the Milwaukee Bucks.

One wouldn't think that veterans like Paul George, Kevin Durant or James Harden would return (or would be made available in a trade), while the Thunder don't have a need for centers like Domantas Sabonis (he played his rookie season with OKC), Al Horford or Steven Adams. Chicago's Josh Giddey is another former member of the Thunder, though such a trade would be a pretty massive splash and is probably unlikely.

Oh, and there's that Russell Westbrook guy who is currently retired...

Regardless, the Thunder now have two spots in the starting lineup they need to address. For the time being, Jared McCain and Ajay Mitchell are likely to do so, with both starting on Monday during a 125-114 win over the Phoenix Suns.

Both are more than capable—Mitchell scored 30 points and added five assists in the win, while McCain chipped in with 18 points and four assists while hitting four threes. But OKC obviously has far less depth in the second unit with both promoted to starting roles.

The Thunder have a mountain of future draft picks, so it won't be surprising if they swing a trade to bolster that depth. Let the speculation begin.

articles.title: 5-Star SF Asa Montgomery Makes Commitment Decision Between Duke, UNC, UConn, LSU and More
articles.summary: Five-star forward Asa Montgomery made his decision, confirming Wednesday to Rivals' Joe Tipton he committed to Duke.
articles.body:
Five-star forward Asa Montgomery made his decision, confirming Wednesday to Rivals' Joe Tipton he committed to Duke.

Montgomery is the No. 8 overall player and third-best small forward in 247Sports' composite rankings for 2027. He's the top-ranked player in the class to have made a commitment so far.

Along with the Blue Devils, the Georgia native made formal visits to Georgia Tech, LSU, North Carolina and UConn.

Montgomery averaged 18.9 points and 10.3 rebounds as a junior at Hillgrove. His production on the EYCL circuit was even better as he led everyone in scoring (27.9 points) while hauling in 10.2 boards over 14 games.

Montgomery also made a strong impression at the FIBA U17 Basketball World Cup this past summer, putting up 9.7 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.1 assists per contest en route to winning a gold medal. That run included a 23-point outburst in the round of 16 against Cameroon.

247Sports' director of scouting Adam Finkelstein wrote how playing in the EYCL and representing Team USA allowed Montgomery to showcase himself in two very different roles. He enjoyed a lot of offensive freedom with Athletes Of Tomorrow and then had to be a supporting player on the United States.

"Those two experiences provide a range of what he could become in the future, both right away at the next level, and then farther down the road as he continues to develop," Finkelstein said. "At 6'6" with a 6'10" wingspan and naturally broader frame, he's best described as a combo-forward who is transitioning from more of a stretch-four into a bigger wing.

"He's an explosive vertical athlete off two feet who has a good sense of timing, both in transition and as a cutter. He's not necessarily a dynamic creator with the ball in his hands, but he's a consistent shooting threat who can pick-and-pop, attack close-outs, play out of the mid-post, and go to the offensive glass."

Montgomery's stock has risen a lot over the last year. He closed out 2025 at No. 72 in the 247Sports' composite ranking and was 67th in mid-May before climbing into the top 10.

Getting a scholarship offer from Duke solidifies how much he has turned heads.

He's the third player to pledge his future to the Blue Devils, joining 5-star forward Kager Knueppel and Australian guard Luke Paul.

Jon Scheyer and his staff have excelled on the recruiting trail since he succeeded Mike Krzyzewski. Duke has consistently boasted a top-five class with Cameron Williams and Deron Rippey Jr. headlining the 2026 haul.

Montgomery is unlikely to be the last 5-star standout to choose Durham, North Carolina, as his next destination.

articles.title: Pacers star Tyrese Haliburton to miss time with left hamstring strain
articles.summary: The All-Star point guard had just returned to the lineup after missing all of last season rehabilitating a ruptured Achilles tendon.
articles.body:
Indiana Pacers All-Star point guard Tyrese Haliburton has suffered a mild left hamstring strain and will miss at least two weeks recovering, head coach Rick Carlisle said on Wednesday afternoon.

Haliburton is being considered week-to-week, though an update isn't expected for at least two weeks. A clearer timeline for his return is not yet known.

Haliburton has had issues with that left hamstring before. He strained it while slipping on a drive to the basket during a game against the Boston Celtics in January of 2024 , costing him 10 games; he'd manage that injury for the rest of the regular season, before re-aggravating it during the Eastern Conference finals against Boston four months later. The following season, he left a January contest against the Cleveland Cavaliers early with left hamstring tightness , and missed the Pacers' following game, too.

The 26-year-old point guard missed all of the 2025-26 regular season after rupturing his right Achilles tendon during Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals . He played in the Pacers' first four games of the 2026-27 campaign, and is averaging 21.8 points, 9.5 assists and 4.5 rebounds in 33 minutes per game, shooting 51.6% from the field, 37% from 3-point range and 86.7% from the free-throw line.

After an emotional return to the lineup in a win over the New Orleans Pelicans, Haliburton appeared to be fully back in the fold for a Pacers team that had looked all but bereft without him last season. He put up 20-and-10 double-doubles in two of his first three games back, leading Indiana to wins in New Orleans and Brooklyn.

Haliburton pressed to play in the second half of Indiana's first back-to-back set of the season, when the Pacers traveled to his native Wisconsin to take on the rival Milwaukee Bucks. He logged a season-high 35 minutes in the Pacers' 110-102 loss ; he was seen wearing a heating pad on his left hamstring while seated on the Indiana bench.

After the back-to-back, Haliburton had been listed as questionable for the Pacers' Wednesday game against the Philadelphia 76ers with left hamstring tightness/soreness — one of eight Indiana players on the injury report , and the third dealing specifically with a hamstring ailment, joining Aaron Nesmith and T.J. McConnell, who has yet to play this season.

The Pacers will be without Haliburton, McConnell, starting center Ivica Zubac (left ankle sprain) and reserve wings Ben Sheppard and Johnny Furphy against Philly on Wednesday. Guard Andrew Nembhard (neck soreness) is also listed as questionable.

Amid this spate of early-season injuries, Indiana has opened the season 2-2, with the NBA's No. 16 offense and No. 14 defense . The Pacers have outscored opponents by four points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions with Haliburton on the floor , and have been outscored by 7.4 points-per-100 with him off it — the largest on-off swing on the team . Some of that stems from the other absences up and down the roster, most notably to backup point guard McConnell; some of it, though, highlights just how central and critical a figure Haliburton is to Indiana's chances of success.

The early woes call to mind the raft of injuries that Indiana suffered at the start of the 2024-25 season, contributing to a rocky start that saw Haliburton and Co. sitting at 10-15 in early December. Once the Pacers got healthy, though, they took off, blossoming into one of the NBA's best teams on both ends of the floor and eventually making it all the way to Game 7 of the Finals. This year's model will hope to follow in its predecessors' footsteps, with Pascal Siakam and the reserve corps holding down the fort until the ailing bodies — and specifically Haliburton's — can get back to full strength and full speed.

Haliburton is the latest in a string of stars to suffer injuries in the early days of this NBA season, joining the likes of Anthony Edwards , Jaren Jackson Jr. , Kawhi Leonard , Jalen Williams , Jalen Duren and Paolo Banchero .

articles.title: Ernie Johnson Announces Final Season with 'Inside the NBA,' Updates Retirement Plans in Video
articles.summary: Legendary broadcaster Ernie Johnson announced Wednesday he's stepping away from Inside the NBA after the 2026-27 season.
articles.body:
Legendary broadcaster Ernie Johnson announced Wednesday he's stepping away from Inside the NBA after the 2026-27 season.

"Just to be clear, I'm not retiring," Johnson said. "Just cutting back. I'll still do March Madness and other projects for TNT and CBS, and I've just started a new production company called 32 Bowties geared toward telling feel-good stories in sports. So this is by no means the end. It's just a turning of the page."

Charles Barkley, Kenny Smith and Shaquille O'Neal gave their emotional reaction to the news on Wednesday's show.

Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić was also among the many NBA players and athletes to react to the news:

NBA commissioner Adam Silver commended Johnson for his "brilliance as a broadcaster" in a statement.

"Few people have shaped the way fans experience the NBA as profoundly as Ernie Johnson," Silver said . "His brilliance as a broadcaster is matched by his character, compassion and generosity, which have been evident throughout his 37 years as host of 'Inside the NBA.' We are grateful for Ernie's extraordinary impact on our league and look forward to celebrating him during his final season."

Johnson has worked in the media since 1979. The 70-year-old first joined Turner Sports in 1989 and went on to contribute to coverage for some of the biggest events in sports including Wimbledon, the Winter Olympics, FIFA World Cup, and the MLB and NBA playoffs.

Johnson is a six-time Sports Emmy Award winner and entered the Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame in 2023.

Hosting Inside the NBA is Johnson's most enduring role and the one for which he's most synonymous. He has deftly played the straight man alongside Smith and Hall of Famers Barkley and O'Neal.

Ask any NBA fan and they're likely to have a go-to Inside clip they often return to.

Maybe it was O'Neal and Barkley's incredulous reaction to reports of a "police presence" during a 2018 altercation between members of the Houston Rockets and Los Angeles Clippers.

There was the time when not even Johnson could keep a straight face as an increasingly frustrated O'Neal vented about Barkley eating into his TV time.

And the quartet still have their fastball. Last week provided perhaps the best "Who He Play For!?" segment of all time as Barkley struggled to name the correct teams for some NBA journeymen.

The show has maintained the same identity following its move from TNT to ESPN. Soon, it will truly be embarking on a new era with Johnson stepping away.

articles.title: Heat Share Photo of Bam Adebayo, Erik Spoelstra 'Figuring It Out' amid 0-4 Start to Giannis Era
articles.summary: Searching for answers amid an 0-4 start to the season, the Miami Heat shared an image of head coach Erik Spoelstra and Bam Adebayo talking things over.
articles.body:
Searching for answers amid an 0-4 start to the season, the Miami Heat shared an image of head coach Erik Spoelstra and Bam Adebayo talking things over.

The Heat posted on the image on X Wednesday, along with the caption: "Figuring it out."

This is the first 0-4 start for the Heat since Pat Riley's final season as head coach in 2007-08. That team lost its first five games en route to a 15-67 finish.

There's a lot to figure out in Miami right now. The dynamic with Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo has not at all worked out the way anyone expected so far.

The Heat have a net rating of minus-31.6 with Adebayo and Antetokounmpo on the floor together.

That's the fifth-worst net rating among all two-man lineups that have played at least 70 minutes together. The only four two-man lineups worse than the Adebayo-Antetokounmpo pairing are also from the Heat, which speaks to how disastrous things have been thus far.

The only teams with a worse net rating than Miami's minus-13.5 mark are the winless Sacramento Kings (minus-17.0) and one-win Chicago Bulls (minus-18.3).

Adebayo's individual performance has been jarring. The three-time All-Star is shooting a career-low 40.0 percent from the field (16.7 percent from three) and is averaging 11.8 points per game, his fewest since the 2018-19 season.

The upside is Adebayo's track record suggests things will get better with a larger sample size, but this has been a huge disappointment for the Heat after their offseason acquisition of Antetokounmpo.

Spoelstra, Adebayo and the Heat will look to get in the win column for the first time this season on Wednesday when they take on the Atlanta Hawks at State Farm Arena.

articles.title: Can these Timberwolves keep pace in the West without Anthony Edwards?
articles.summary: Minnesota's massive summertime pivot was working before its superstar went down with a knee injury.
articles.body:
The whole idea behind the Minnesota Timberwolves' massive summertime pivot — out go Julius Randle and Naz Reid, in comes LaMelo Ball — was to find a way to reduce the ball-handling and shot-creation workload on Anthony Edwards, and allow the four-time All-Star to do what he does best: put the ball in the basket, again and again and again. And through four games of the 2026-27 NBA season, it was working .

Edwards opened the season on fire, scoring more points per game than anybody besides Luka Dončić, while shooting 54% on 2-pointers and 40% from long distance. He's been at his most efficient with Ball setting him up, posting an absurd 75% true shooting percentage (which factors in 2-point, 3-point and free-throw accuracy) with Ball on the floor , 20 percentage points above his career average; LaMelo-to-Ant has produced more baskets (10) than any other assist combination in the league thus far.

The Wolves enter Wednesday's matchup with the Golden State Warriors owning the NBA's No. 4 offense and leading the league in both pull-up field-goal attempts and pull-up shooting efficiency , with Edwards and Ball leading the way. Minnesota is scoring a scorching 126.8 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions with its new-look backcourt on the floor, opening the season with three blowout wins and an overtime loss against a Cleveland Cavaliers squad that just made the Eastern Conference finals.

This, broadly, is the formula that the Wolves believed would give them the brand of firepower necessary to be able to more effectively stand toe-to-toe with the likes of the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs, who have eliminated them from the last two postseasons. It's a formula, however, that requires Edwards to remain upright and ambulatory … and, as we learned on Tuesday, that's something he's not going to be for a while .

Just four games into the season, Edwards needs arthroscopic surgery on his right knee — the same knee in which he experienced recurring issues last season with what's called patellofemoral pain syndrome, or "runner's knee." That ailment cost the All-NBA guard 11 of the Wolves' final 14 games of the regular season; he needed to have his right knee drained multiple times during Minnesota's playoff run , too. (He also hyperextended his left knee during the opening round against the Denver Nuggets; he missed just two games, and averaged 23.7 points on 47/38/80 shooting splits after returning.)

After spending the bulk of the summer resting up to give that knee time to properly heal , and reportedly feeling fully healthy and operational through Minnesota's training camp and preseason slate, Edwards reportedly tweaked his knee during the Wolves' opening-night win over the Miami Heat. You'd be forgiven for not noticing, considering he hung 45 and drilled nine 3-pointers to ruin Giannis Antetokounmpo's South Beach debut:

Despite the tweak, Edwards played on, with observers noticing frequent grimacing , instinctive reaches for that right knee , and the occasional limp. But while he was listed as questionable heading into Monday's matchup with the Cavaliers, Edwards not only played, but logged 41 minutes, had more total touches ( 82 ) and a higher time of possession ( nine minutes ) than any other player in the game, and finished nearly 40% of Minnesota's offensive possessions with a shot attempt, foul drawn or turnover — a usage rate that would've been a top-five mark for him in each of the last four seasons — all on the second night of a back-to-back.

In fairness, he did look awfully good while doing so …

… and the Wolves, it seems, didn't suspect that there was anything more significant going on than the kind of soreness through which superstars of Edwards' caliber are often expected to play.

"It's a daily situation," Wolves head coach Chris Finch told reporters before the Cavs game. "I don't think there's any long-term concern."

Concerns mounted after the game, though, with subsequent imaging showing "increased issues there," according to ESPN's Shams Charania — damage "that was different from what he experienced against the San Antonio Spurs in May," according to Jon Krawczynski of The Athletic.

"It's not a meniscus," Wolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly told reporters at the team's Wednesday shootaround session. "It's just a — I don't want to speak out of school. My liberal arts degree will screw me up. It's just an arthroscopic clean-up of his knee. … We've had a bunch of imaging since the summer, and it changed as of yesterday."

Based on that new information, player and team elected to move forward with a surgical procedure on Thursday, from which Sarah Todd of the Minnesota Star Tribune reports that the Wolves "hope to have [Edwards] back on the court sometime in December." That might be a tad optimistic. Krawczynski pegs Edwards' return as more likely to be in January : "As of now, the belief is it's going to be more than two months ."

Two months from Thursday would be Dec. 29. The Wolves' final game of 2026 comes on New Year's Eve at home against the Denver Nuggets. If Edwards is back for that, he would have missed 28 games, ensuring that, for the second consecutive year , he'll be ineligible for year-end awards like Most Valuable Player and the All-NBA teams, and for the supermax salary escalators on his next extension that would come if he were to receive them.

The message coming out of Minnatlantasota , though, is that Ant is focused less on putting himself in position to make the top dollar next summer than giving himself the best chance to reach the top of the mountain this spring.

"Like we've talked about before, there's only one thing that matters to Ant," Justin Holland, Edwards' business manager, said in a statement to The Athletic . "It's not about individual accolades, All-NBAs or anything like that. It's a single focus: winning a championship. We've seen in a short time what this team is capable of, and know big things are ahead when all are 100%."

That could be especially true in a Western Conference in which the Thunder will likely be without starters Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace for most, if not all, of the regular season , and in which a Spurs team that opened up with losses to Oklahoma City and Houston might have some kinks to iron out as they look to return to the NBA Finals. If the expected powerhouses have more cracks in the armor than might have been anticipated, and if Edwards and the Wolves believe that what they put on tape during those first four games is real, then nothing matters more than entering the postseason as close to full strength as possible — even if that means putting Edwards on ice.

"With Anthony, all he wants to do is compete, so he's doing this kicking and screaming," Connelly said Wednesday. "But we're pretty confident that he'll get out there when he's right. We don't know when it's going to be, but we don't think it's going to be something that's going to cost him the season. … The best thing about what he's gonna go under is, he'll be as good as new. It's not something we're concerned with long term."

Of course, the rest of the Wolves still have to make it through these next two months without falling too far off the pace in the West. You don't just replace a player who can average more than 30 points per game while soaking up nearly 40% of the team's offensive possessions; it'll be interesting to see how Finch rebalances the books to keep Minnesota's attack humming.

You'd expect Jaden McDaniels, who saw his per-possession scoring and usage rate both climb last season when he wasn't playing alongside Edwards — and who opened eyebrows with his 32-point, 10-rebound performance to close out Denver in Game 6 of the opening round with Edwards sidelined — to play a larger finishing role, too. You'd expect Ball — who, through four games, is scoring, shooting and using a lower share of his team's offensive possessions than he has since his rookie year in Charlotte — to scale his usage back up toward the No. 1 option levels of his latter years with the Hornets.

You'd expect the Wolves to push the pace even more, too. Minnesota has gotten out in transition less frequently in recent years with Edwards on the floor than when he sits , and a more Ball-centric approach would seem to be one oriented more toward hitting the gas than to patiently probing in the half-court.

"I think it's more pace now," reserve guard Bones Hyland told reporters on Wednesday. "More running, a lot more up-and-down, and a lot more excitement as well. A lot of players stepping up. We got a lot of versatility, so I think it's gonna be good for us."

Ayo Dosunmu, recipient of a nine-figure contract this summer , will likely slide into the starting lineup and shoulder some of the shot-creation workload. Jonathan Kuminga, off to such a strong start doing the dirty work as a complementary two-way power forward, could be asked to step into more shots. Finch will need more from reserves like Hyland, Terrence Shannon Jr., Jaylen Clark and, frankly, everyone else — including Rudy Gobert and Joan Beringer, the back-line anchors of a defense that will have to remain among the NBA's elite for the Wolves to consistently notch Ws in the absence of their most dangerous offensive weapon.

Edwards, evidently, is confident in their ability to hold down the fort without a top-10 player in the world. It's kind of ironic: What Edwards saw in these first four games made him believe enough in the potential of who the Wolves could grow to be that he's willing to sacrifice the next couple of months in hopes of maximizing their opportunity of reaching that vaulted ceiling.

articles.title: Philadelphia 76ers vs. Indiana Pacers Live NBA Updates, Scores and Highlights
articles.summary: Both the Philadelphia 76ers and Indiana Pacers are looking to rebound from losses when they meet at Gainbridge Fieldhouse on Wednesday. Indy's search for the win will have to come with a skeleton crew.
articles.body:
Ben Sheppard recently underwent surgery for a torn meniscus in his left knee. Head coach Rick Carlisle saying he needed a "full" repair as opposed to a partial one suggests we won't see him again before the All-Star break.

Though Sheppard isn't what you'd consider a core player, he's a rotation staple who brings capable wing defense to the table. Without him, Indiana will have to rely more on Quenton Jackson, Kelly Oubre Jr. and Jarace Walker.

articles.title: New NBA Trade Rumors Update Herb Jones, Trey Murphy III Buzz Amid Pelicans Struggles
articles.summary: A New Orleans Pelicans official told NBA insider Marc Stein that the team hasn't "indicated a willingness" to trade Herb Jones amidst a 3-0 start to the season, with Jones averaging just 17 minutes per game off the bench thus far.
articles.body:
A New Orleans Pelicans official told NBA insider Marc Stein that the team hasn't "indicated a willingness" to trade Herb Jones amidst a 3-0 start to the season, with Jones averaging just 17 minutes per game off the bench thus far.

Stein added that the Pelicans have "maintained a high threshold on trade interest in Trey Murphy III and Jones for months."

Jones, 28, is only averaging 3.3 points and two rebounds per game thus far in the 2026-27 campaign, though he is shooting 40 percent from three and remains an impactful defensive wing.

Porziņģis Trade Idea Best For Warriors 💡

"Herb is the ultimate professional," head coach Jamahl Mosley told reporters Tuesday when asked about Jones' decrease in minutes. "Finding more time for him is going to be a key priority for me. I know that, as a defensive coach. ... We talked about [evaluating the team] in a five-game sample size."

The 26-year-old Murphy, on the other hand, remains one of the team's starters and is putting up 15.3 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.7 assists per game, shooting 41.2 percent from three. There would obviously be plenty of interest around the league if he was put on the trade market, though he remains an important part of the team's core alongside Zion Williamson, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears, among others.

Just how precious the Pelicans should be keeping that group together is debatable, however. New Orleans has had two playoff appearances in the past eight years and is coming off back-to-back seasons with less than 30 wins. This season's rough start hasn't inspired much confidence that the team is about to reverse that trend.

But for now, the Pelicans are maintaining the status quo. By February's trade deadline, that stance might change.

articles.title: Ja Morant Reacts to Facing Grizzlies for 1st Time Since Blazers Trade, 'Not a Big Grudge Guy'
articles.summary: Ja Morant spent the first seven years of his NBA career with the Memphis Grizzlies and quickly established himself as one of the franchise's most beloved players.
articles.body:
Ja Morant spent the first seven years of his NBA career with the Memphis Grizzlies and quickly established himself as one of the franchise's most beloved players.

But his final season with the team saw him at odds with the coaching staff, and he was ultimately traded to the Portland Trail Blazers this offseason.

On Thursday, he'll go up against his former team for the first time, and he won't be harboring any negative feelings.

"Nothing harsh from me for Memphis," Morant said, per The Athletic's Jason Quick . "At all."

Morant said that he's "not a big grudge guy," and the game against the Grizzlies will be "just another basketball game on the schedule." He added that he still keeps in touch with some of his former teammates and watches their games.

Morant specifically seemed to have disdain for head coach Tuomas Iisalo, earning a one-game suspension for comments made about him in November last year. But he seems to have left those feelings in the past.

"I'm cool with everybody over there," Morant said. "I don't got no hard feelings with nobody, unless they got it with me."

Morant and the Blazers are off to a 3-0 start, and he's putting up 16.3 points and 6.3 assists per game. But his former team is also thriving without him, as Memphis is 4-0 heading into the contest against Portland.

articles.title: WNBA Finals Game 6: Attrition, fatigue, focus take center stage in longest Finals ever
articles.summary: The Valkyries can close out the series in Game 6 in Atlanta, but the matchup with the Dream will be about more than just X's and O's.
articles.body:
COLLEGE PARK, Ga. — DeWanna Bonner, the most experienced postseason player in WNBA league history, definitely feels the difference. The mental and physical fatigue, elevated by a cross-country matchup, is setting in ahead of the first Finals Game 6 in league history.

In the longest WNBA Finals since moving to a best-of-seven format last year — and after the league's second 44-game regular season — even the most experienced are in new waters. Bonner, a two-time champion before joining the Atlanta Dream in August, knows it comes down to how a team channels it. At this point, three-time Las Vegas Aces champion and Game 5 Golden State Valkyries catalyst Kiah Stokes doesn't see it as an X's and O's game. There's too much knowledge for that.

"You're seeing the same team over and over and over again," Stokes said. "It just gets to the point where at this time it's, 'Who wants it more?'"

This is a game that could hinge on emotions. There's a pure will to closing out a team on the road and a required hunger for the home squad to keep its season alive. The mental edge, which shifted over the course of the series, will be key.

The Dream trash-talked through the first three, taking back-to-back wins for a fragile 2-1 series lead. The Valkyries began returning some of the fire, rattling off their own two-fer and a commanding 3-2 series lead.

Angel Reese, the Dream's motor in both play and trash talk, said after going up 2-1 they were tracking how well the team was getting under the Valkyries' skin. She said Wednesday she isn't thinking about whether the trash talk ratcheted up over the last few games.

The Dream still have the same mindset they had a week ago when they returned to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4, she said. It simply needs to be emphasized and utilized in a must-win situation. Because this is where she always lives.

"I don't think that headspace has ever changed in my life," Reese said. "This is the mentality and how I approach the game, every game."

Reese's offensive production dropped in the back-to-back losses. She scored 65 points, shooting 22 of 39 (56%) from the floor in the first three games compared to 15 points on 4 for 20 (20%) in the next two. Her 3-pointers are a barometer of the Dream's success (they're 15-0 when she makes one), a stat she wants to maximize. She missed one in Game 4, and had an open look early but for the first time in the playoffs did not attempt one in Game 5.

Atlanta turned the ball over 35 times in Games 4 and 5, nearly identical to the 36 in the first three games. The Dream's 62 and 55 points, respectively, were season lows, and they have shot at least 34% from the floor only once this series, bursting out for a 49.3% showing in the 97-71 win in Game 4 at State Farm Arena.

The Valkyries' bounceback came with two full days between games. Coach Natalie Nakase used a first-time starting lineup and shortened the rotation on a team that led the league by a wide margin in bench points. The Dream also had two full days to watch film and adjust, although that included a travel day Tuesday.

"You're always locked in when it comes to the Finals," Dream head coach Karl Smesko said. "But when the other team can close out a series and you're down to that last one, I think there's even another level that everybody can get to that they didn't even know they could."

The Dream are the more inexperienced team, led by Bonner and two-time champion point guard Jordin Canada. Reese reiterated a few times on Wednesday that it's her and many of her teammates' first Finals.

The Valkyries can lean on more. Kayla Thornton won with New York when the 2024 Finals went to a deciding Game 5. Cecilia Zandalasini sat on the other side with the Minnesota Lynx. Stokes has played a fair share of closeout games, nearly all with Nakase when the Valkyries head coach was an assistant in Las Vegas.

No matter the length of the series, there are aspects that remain the same.

"This is going to be our toughest battle, both physically and mentally," Nakase said Wednesday. "We're facing a desperate team, and any team that's desperate, they're going to scrap for rebounds, they're going to hit on screens, they're going to dive on loose balls, and we have to match that. If not, we have to be better."

The Valkyries learned last time they were in town how to communicate better amid a loud 17,000-plus State Farm Arena crowd that features musical performances during timeouts. Game 6 will be played there after it was moved out of prime time to accommodate the venue change. Atlanta's usual home arena is 3,500-seat Gateway Center. Tipoff is scheduled for 12:30 p.m. ET.

Dream ownership wrote an open letter to fans on Tuesday night that a midday Thursday tip was "not what we would have chosen and not what we fought for." The players have stayed out of discussing the controversy, instead redirecting comments toward the crowd they expect at what will be their full-time home next year.

"This is the moment that we need to come and maximize," Reese said. "We're not just here just to mess around. We're here to play Atlanta Dream basketball [and] get back to our identity. We've watched a lot of positive things and a lot of feel-goods, which is what we need coming back home."

articles.title: Legendary host Ernie Johnson announces he is stepping away from 'Inside the NBA' after this season
articles.summary: After 37 seasons hosting "Inside the NBA," legendary host Ernie Johnson said he's stepping away from the show, saying that "it's just time."
articles.body: Legendary "Inside the NBA" host Ernie Johnson announced Wednesday on X that he will step away from the show after the 2026-27 NBA season. Johnson, 70, revealed in the video that he has dealt with heart issues and underwent bypass surgery 14 months ago. He said he wants to slow down and spend more time with his wife and five grandchildren. "I've been hosting 'Inside the NBA’ for a long time. This is my 37th year, and I've long described it as a get-to job. Still amazed that I get to do this for a living. Now, as the years have gone by and I turned 70 this past summer, folks have asked me, 'So, how long are you going to keep doing Inside?' Well, I want to take a couple of minutes of your time to answer that. This will be my last season. Totally my decision. It's just time," Johnson said in his video. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Johnson clarified that he is not retiring from broadcasting entirely, only from "Inside the NBA." The broadcaster said he recently launched a production company, 32 Bow Ties, and plans to continue working on March Madness coverage and other projects for TNT and CBS . "So why now? Total honesty here. I've always prided myself on my preparation, the hours I put in every day getting ready for the next show. I've always loved that part of my job, but I've always vowed that if that ever became more of a challenge than it is a joy, then I'll know it's time to step away. And now after 37 seasons, it's time," Johnson said. He cited his heart issues and his desire to spend time with family as a contributing factor in his decision. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "This isn't a case where my doctor said, ‘You need to stop working.’ It's nothing like that. But here's the deal. Going through that has made me treasure even more every second with my amazing wife of 44 years, Cheryl, and being Poppy to our five grandchildren. So, I just want to slow down a bit, spend more time I'm enjoying that," Johnson said. He said it has been an honor to work for decades alongside Shaquille O’Neal (who joined the show in 2011), Charles Barkley (2000) and Kenny Smith (1998). Johnson joined "Inside the NBA" in 1990, one year after its creation. Johnson is not the only "Inside the NBA" personality planning to retire after the 2026-27 season. Barkley announced last month that the season would be his last. So, this is by no means the end. It's just a turning of the page. And I'll forever cherish every chapter we have written with inside the NBA," Johnson said. "And lastly, I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support, and on this day for your understanding. We'll see you on TV tonight."

articles.title: El Valencia Basket se estrena aplastando al débil Rapid Bucaresti
articles.standfirst: Bibby (22+5+2), Araujo (15+6+5) y Peterson (13+2+6) lideran la paliza a las rumanas (105-47)
articles.summary: Bibby (22+5+2), Araujo (15+6+5) y Peterson (13+2+6) lideran la paliza a las rumanas (105-47)
articles.body: El Valencia Basket sumó este miércoles su primera victoria en la Euroliga, en la tercera jornada de la fase de grupos, en el Roig Arena, al superar con holgura al Rapid de Bucarest con un gran acierto exterior que le llevó a batir su récord de triples anotados en un partido con 20 y con la interior Chloe Bibby como principal referencia con 22 puntos. El Valencia Basket trató de imponer su superioridad física ante un Rapid de Bucarest que solo contaba con una pívot y saltó con un quinteto con tres jugadoras interiores, aunque los primeros puntos llegaron desde el triple y desde la velocidad de la base Alexis Peterson. La altura del Valencia Basket obligaba a las rumanas a jugar lejos del aro y a lanzar con rapidez para sumar, algo que no parecía preocuparles. Con un triple de Bianca Voica dejaba la diferencia en solo 2 puntos en el ecuador del primer parcial (13-11, min.5). Un espeso Valencia Basket comenzó a despegar con los cambios. Entre Helena Pueyo y Virag Takacs-Kiss anotaron 9 puntos consecutivos castigando tanto dentro como fuera y la diferencia solo hacía que aumentar. Más todavía cuando María Araújo anotó el quinto triple en ocho intentos antes del bocinazo final del primer cuarto (30-15, min.10). El parcial para las 'taronja' llegó a ser de 17-4 y empezaba a confirmar la teórica superioridad local. Y por si fuera poco, al acierto exterior se unió la solidez defensiva. El Valencia Basket aprovechó su ventaja interior para incomodar los ataques de un Rapid de Bucarest incapaz de anotar o bien por su desacierto o bien por los tapones que recibían sus jugadoras. Ante un inofensivo Bucarest, al Valencia Basket le valía para vivir de los 6 puntos seguidos de Chloe Bibby mantener su ventaja cerca de los 20 puntos (36-19, min.15). De nuevo con los cambios, el Valencia Basket mantuvo la energía defensiva alta y también el acierto exterior. Los triples de Isabel Hernandez y de Kiss llevaron a superar la veintena de puntos de diferencia ante un equipo rumano que solo pudo anotar 7 puntos en 10 minutos. El partido, prácticamente decidido a favor del conjunto local al descanso, encontró en la diferencia de puntos final su principal argumento con toda la segunda parte por jugar (54-22, min.20). El Valencia Basket saltó con la intención de lograr la máxima ventaja posible y haciendo uso de su acierto exterior continuó castigando una y otra vez. En solo tres minutos había sumado 11 puntos con los triples de Bibby, Araújo y Peterson. En un intento de frenar la sangría y mantener la energía, el Rapid de Bucarest cambió a una defensa zonal que en su primera actuación se llevó otro triple más, de Pueyo, y una diferencia que ya alcanzó los 40 puntos (70-30, min.25). Con todo a favor, el Valencia Basket bajó su actividad defensiva y el Bucarest lo aprovechó para tirar de orgullo y agitar su casillero de puntos con la pívot Nicolett Orban para tratar de maquillar el resultado, algo imposible ante el vendaval anotador de las 'taronja'. El entrenador del Valencia Basket, Javi Torralba, aprovechó que todo estaba decidido para darle protagonismo a las canteranas Isabel Hernández y Marina Bleda y para que Bibby, fichada la semana pasada, siguiera acumulando minutos con sus nuevas compañeras en una noche en la que fue despedida a gritos de 'MVP' tras ser la máxima anotadora de su equipo. La fiesta fue completa cuando un triple de Marta Suárez actualizó los registros históricos de triples anotados en un partido del Valencia Basket al superar los 18 convertidos en el partido de la jornada 26 de la Liga Femenina Endesa de la pasada temporada ante el Spar Gran Canaria. 105 - Valencia Basket (30+24+24+27): Peterson (13), Balogun (8), Araújo (15), Carrera (4), Bibby (22) -cinco titular- Kiss (9), Hernández (4), Suárez (13), Bleda (4), Buenavida (-), Pueyo (13). 47 - Rapid de Bucarest (15+7+15+10): Cuic (16), Delic (8), Orban (7), Palenikova (7), Voica (3) -cinco titular- Tanase (-), Nan (6), Ghizila (-), Zane (-), Mbaka (-). Árbitros: Veronika Obertova, Pawel Pacek y Vladimir Zanev. Sin eliminadas. Incidencias: partido correspondiente a la tercera jornada de la fase de grupos de la Euroliga femenina disputado en el pabellón Roig Arena ante 2.656 espectadores. Antes del inicio se guardó un minuto de silencio en memoria de las víctimas del accidente ferroviario de Toledo.

articles.title: El San Pablo Burgos cae ante el Rigas Zelli y no levanta cabeza
articles.standfirst: Steward (18+3+2) y Taboada (16+4+4) no evitan la derrota ante los letones (71-79)
articles.summary: Steward (18+3+2) y Taboada (16+4+4) no evitan la derrota ante los letones (71-79)
articles.body: El Recoletas Salud San Pablo Burgos cayó este miércoles ante el Rigas Zelli (71-79) en un encuentro de la Eurocopa en el que las pérdidas de balón y las dificultades defensivas condenaron al conjunto dirigido por Porfi Fisac. Pese a los intentos de reacción de los burgaleses, el acierto exterior y la mayor regularidad del equipo letón terminaron por decantar un partido en el que los locales fueron a remolque durante buena parte de la segunda mitad. El conjunto burgalés comenzó adelantándose en el marcador, pero las pérdidas de balón permitieron al Rigas Zelli tomar rápidamente el control del encuentro. Los visitantes aprovecharon los errores locales para abrir una primera brecha (5-15), que obligó a Porfi Fisac a solicitar un tiempo muerto. El San Pablo encontró en los tiros libres la fórmula para reducir diferencias (11-15) y, con una notable mejoría en los últimos minutos, consiguió darle la vuelta al marcador gracias a un parcial de 10-2 que le permitió cerrar el primer cuarto por delante (21-17). El equipo letón reaccionó en el segundo periodo apoyándose en su intensidad defensiva, que dificultó la circulación de balón de los burgaleses. Los de Fisac trataron de mantener el ritmo anotador para conservar su ventaja (30-29), pero la aparición de Ivan Tkachenko permitió a los visitantes recuperar la iniciativa y marcharse al descanso con cuatro puntos de renta (35-39). El paso por los vestuarios no cambió la dinámica del encuentro, el Rigas Zelli regresó con mayor intensidad y firmó un parcial de 2-10 que elevó su ventaja hasta los doce puntos (37-49), la máxima diferencia hasta ese momento. El San Pablo intentó reaccionar de la mano de Joaquín Taboada, que asumió protagonismo ofensivo para mantener a los suyos en el partido, pero el acierto desde el perímetro de los letones frustró cualquier intento de remontada. Los visitantes conservaron el control y afrontaron los últimos diez minutos con ocho puntos de ventaja (54-62). El último cuarto mantuvo el mismo guion, el San Pablo buscó reducir distancias con las acciones ofensivas de DJ Steward, pero sus problemas defensivos le impidieron encadenar las paradas necesarias para acercarse en el marcador. El Rigas Zelli continuó encontrando situaciones cómodas de anotación y volvió a ampliar su renta (60-71), dejando prácticamente sentenciado el encuentro. Pese a los esfuerzos finales de los burgaleses, el conjunto letón administró su ventaja hasta certificar la victoria por 71-79. 71 - San Pablo Burgos (21+14+19+17): DJ Steward (18), Ziga Samar (2), Christian Sengfelder (7), Sekou Doumbouya (3) Joaquín Taboada (16) -cinco inicial - Chase Audige (7), Balsa Koprivica (2), Pablo Almazán (0), Dani Díez (5), Rubén Guerrero (0), Dusan Radosavljevic (9) y Raúl Lobaco (3). 79 - Rigas Zelli (17+22+23+17): Benjamín Shungu (13), Tyler Wahl (12), Rolands Sulcs (6), Klavs Cavars (2), Ivan Tkachenko (15) -cinco inicial- Tony Perkins (2), Toms Skuja (2), Ody Oguama (6), Martynas Varnas (15), Tomas Talcis (-), Janis Berzins (6). Árbitros: Milivoje Jovcic, Kerem Baki, Edoardo Gonella Incidencias: Partido correspondiente a la jornada 5 del Grupo A de Eurocup celebrado en el Coliseum Burgos ante 6.896 espectadores.

articles.title: New Kyrie Irving Trade Rumors on Heat Links, Interest in Mavs Star Amid 2026-27 NBA Season
articles.summary: Multiple teams are interested in Dallas Mavericks star Kyrie Irving on the trade market as the 2026-27 season begins, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.
articles.body:
Multiple teams are interested in Dallas Mavericks star Kyrie Irving on the trade market as the 2026-27 season begins, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

"There's a slew of teams now that are monitoring Kyrie Irving," Charania reported during a Wednesday appearance on the Pat McAfee Show (8:00 mark).

Blockbuster Trade to Fix Miami's Bam Problem 💡

Charania also discussed the Miami Heat as a potential landing spot for Irving.

"I'm sure knowing the Heat, they're going to be monitoring Kyrie Irving," Charania reported (11:00 mark). "But there's gonna be several teams interested in Kyrie Irving. The question is if you're Miami, what can you give for Kyrie Irving? You already traded away three first-round picks and a swap and other assets to go get Giannis Antetokounmpo to bring to this team."

"So, what can you trade right now? I believe they have one first-round pick eligible to be traded," he added. "Is that enough to get Kyrie Irving? My sense is probably not."

Irving will earn $39.5 million for the 2026-27 season before he has a $42.4 million player option for his 2027-28 campaign.

The 34-year-old has remained an efficient isolation scorer after recovering from a torn ACL , averaging 19.0 points per game on 51.2/32.0/100.0 shooting splits in his first three appearances this season.

Still, Irving doesn't fit the exact timeline of a Mavericks squad looking to build around 19-year-old Cooper Flagg moving forward.

Dallas currently sits at 2-2, but could become willing to discuss swaps involving Irving if it falls out of the Western Conference postseason picture.

The trade deadline for the 2026-27 season is on Feb. 11.

articles.title: Lakers Sign Center to 2-Way Deal Amid Depth Concerns
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Lakers signed center Lawson Lovering to a two-way deal as their problems with depth behind Walker Kessler reveal themselves. The post Lakers...
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Lakers signed center Lawson Lovering to a two-way deal as their problems with depth behind Walker Kessler reveal themselves.

Lovering, 23, went undrafted in 2025, spending most of last season with the Memphis Grizzlies' G League affiliate. He played 13 games in the G League, averaging 8.9 points and 7.8 rebounds per game with the team. The Grizzlies brought him on for a 10-day contract in February, and he featured twice for the team—starting once.

He averaged seven points and 7.5 rebounds per game across his two appearances in the NBA, also logging 1.5 assists and two steals and blocks per game.

A seven-footer, Lovering offers some size for the Lakers if they choose to use him, as he would be the team's second player clocking in at or over seven feet tall, the other being starting center Walker Kessler.

Who has Been Playing Behind Walker Kessler So Far?

The Lakers don't have too many options behind Kessler, with center Kevon Looney and forward Sandro Mamukelashvili spending most of the time at the position while Kessler sits. Jarred Vanderbilt is also available for the Lakers off of the bench, but is still yet to feature this season despite being on a $12 million contract.

Kessler is averaging 31.5 minutes per game, the third most on the team behind Austin Reaves and Luka Doncic, which has prompted overuse concerns after he spent last year on the sidelines with an injury.

The Lakers' rebounding is struggling due to their lack of depth, as they currently rank dead last in the league in total rebounds and have been out-rebounded in half of their games—allowing the third most in the NBA so far.

Lovering could provide some relief for the Lakers behind Kessler with his size, and is a low-risk signing for the Lakers given his status as a two-way player.

He likely won't be available for the team's game against the Los Angeles Clippers on Wednesday at 7:30 p.m. PT, but could be involved in Friday's game against the Golden State Warriors if head coach JJ Redick sees fit. The Lakers will have to make do with what they have against the Clippers, though, and will look to mirror their result against them from earlier in the season.

articles.title: Kobe Bryant's Rare Game-Worn, Signed Air Jordan Shoes from 'Sneaker Free Agency' to Be Auctioned
articles.summary: A pair of game-worn and rare Air Jordan shoes from Kobe Bryant's "sneaker free agency season" during his illustrious career are being auctioned.
articles.body:
A pair of game-worn and rare Air Jordan shoes from Kobe Bryant's "sneaker free agency season" during his illustrious career are being auctioned.

The Realest announced in a press release Wednesday it is auctioning the Air Jordan 8 sneakers that Bryant wore when he led the Los Angeles Lakers to a victory over the Boston Celtics on March 21, 2003. Each shoe features Bryant's signature and No. 8 inscription.

Bryant was signed to Adidas and Nike at different times during his career. However, he was a sneaker free agent during that 2002-03 campaign because he departed from Adidas and was yet to sign with Nike.

He wore different shoes during that season, including these Air Jordan exclusives that were specifically designed for him.

Bryant famously emulated Michael Jordan, especially early in his career. What's more, that 2002-03 season was the final one of His Airness' career.

As for Bryant, he appeared in all 82 games during that sneaker free agency season and finished third in MVP voting as an All-NBA First Team and All-Defensive First Team selection. His Lakers lost in the second round of the playoffs after taking home the previous three championships.

The Hall of Famer helped lead the Lakers to a 104-96 win over the Celtics in the game when he wore this pair of Air Jordan sneakers.

It wasn't a great scoring night, as he finished with 13 points on 5-of-11 shooting from the field. However, he impacted the game in other ways with seven assists, three rebounds, one block and one steal.

And now someone will have the chance to own the shoes he was wearing during the performance.

articles.title: WNBA draft lottery set for Nov. 15, with Houston and Toronto tied for best odds at No. 1 pick
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — The WNBA will have its annual draft lottery on Nov. 15, with Houston and Toronto having the best chances to get the No.
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — The WNBA will have its annual draft lottery on Nov. 15, with Houston and Toronto having the best chances to get the No. 1 pick and potentially JuJu Watkins.

The Comets, who were formerly the Connecticut Sun, have a 33% chance of getting the top choice. Toronto has the same chance. Houston finished 1-2 against Toronto in the 2026 season so the Comets can't fall further than the No. 3 pick. Toronto is guaranteed at least the No. 4 choice at the WNBA draft that will take place on April 12.

Washington has the third-best chance at getting the No. 1 pick, as the Mystics possess the Chicago Sky's first-round choice after a trade. The Mystics have a 16% chance at winning the lottery. Seattle (9.3%), Portland (5.2%) and Los Angeles (3.6% ) are next. The Sparks also own the rights to the Phoenix Mercury's pick.

Toronto and Portland's chances were based off their one year in the league. The other five teams' draft odds were based off their records for the previous two seasons.

The draft will be conducted at 7:30 p.m. EST on Nov. 15 following the UConn-Louisville women's basketball game.

Watkins is coming back from an ACL injury that sidelined her for all of last season. She could come back for another season at USC next year. Other top players who could enter the draft include Hannah Hidalgo of Notre Dame and Madison Booker of Texas.

The NCAA is allowing players a fifth year of eligibility to play, so it's not certain who will enter the draft yet.

articles.title: The Best Tunnel Fits Of The NBA 2026-27 Season: Week 1
articles.summary: It’s the most wonderful time of the year: the NBA season has officially commenced. This week's tunnel looks feature relaxed outfits paired with bold accessor...
articles.body:
It's the most wonderful time of the year: the NBA season has officially commenced. The 2026–27 season is already off to a lively start, with all the lore that's been brewing in the off-season finally making its way to the court. There's been the off-season trades involving Giannis and Tyler Herro, LeBron James's signing with the 76ers, and the return of injured players to the starting lineup, namely Kyrie Irving and Tyrese Haliburton.

Of course, some star teams have had rocky starts, going 0–3 to open the season. The Knicks , fresh off their championship win, stumbled on their home opener and ring ceremony night, alongside the more surprising Golden State Warriors and Miami Heat. But that's just the way the game goes. Through all the early-season chaos, one thing has remained a constant in the NBA: their tunnel fits.

The tunnel has become a hallmark of the game, a ceremony in its own right. Before the warm-up gear goes on, before pregame shootarounds, and even before the all-important player -to-player handshake, athletes first make their walk down the tunnel. During this first week, home openers and all, we're seeing more relaxed fits, pared down with a bold accessory like a bag, satchel, or even a shiny and flashy jacket. While in the past, logos took over the tunnel, and designer brands and bags were integral to a game day fit, we're seeing more symbols of quiet luxury taking over: Celine jeans, Louis Vuitton ties, Gucci glasses, etc. There hasn't been much off-season fashion or beauty lore to speak of, aside from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's fast-growing braids, but we can only assume the players were saving their best style moments for the court.

Below, we've rounded up the best home opener fits, the looks that hit the tunnel before they hit the court. In our hearts, they're all winners.
